title: Add-on therapies
intro: Some medicines and treatments are used with gender-affirming hormone therapy to manage some of its effects. On testosterone, these effects are acne, scalp hair loss, periods that continue, and vaginal dryness. On oestrogen or androgen blockers, they are facial and body hair that stays, scalp hair, and changes in sex drive and erections. None of these is hormone therapy in another form. None is automatic. It is background reading, not a prescription.

body: Hormone therapy changes more than the things you are aiming for. Some effects come up often enough to have their own treatments. Each effect may or may not happen. The medicines used for them are ordinary prescriptions, not hormone therapy in another form [1][2].
Each medicine named here has its own page in the Medicines A–Z with doses, side effects and cost.

easy.text: Other medicines can help with some effects of hormone therapy.
For example: pimples, hair loss, periods, or dryness.
On oestrogen, some people want help with face hair, head hair, or changes in sex drive or erections.
Ask your doctor which, if any, is right for you.

figure.caption: The effects of hormone therapy that are often treated, and what Australian guidance and product information name for each. Based on the Australian position statement, Australia's 2026 standards of care, the AJGP hormone therapy article and Australian product information [3][2][4][12][13].

body: These four sections are for people taking testosterone.

Acne on testosterone happens the same way as other acne. Androgens (hormones such as testosterone) make the skin's oil (sebaceous) glands bigger, and they make more oil [5]. More oil means more pimples on the face and body [5]. Acne tends to start in the first few weeks of treatment. It is most active in the first one to two years. After that it often settles, even without treatment [4].

Australian guidance uses the usual steps [4]. The first step is a retinoid and benzoyl peroxide, used together on the skin [4]. If that is not enough, the next step is a tetracycline taken by mouth, such as doxycycline [4]. For severe or scarring acne, the next step is isotretinoin [4]. This is a stronger retinoid taken by mouth. It is usually managed with a dermatologist (skin specialist) [4]. The three work in different ways. The skin treatment clears pores and reduces bacteria on the skin. Doxycycline calms the inflammation (redness and swelling) that follows. Isotretinoin shrinks the oil glands themselves. That is why it is kept for acne the other options have not controlled.

The body turns testosterone into dihydrotestosterone (DHT), using an enzyme called 5-alpha reductase [6]. DHT drives most of the body changes from testosterone. But its effect on hair roots (follicles) depends on where they are [2]. Follicles on the beard, underarms and pubic area grow larger. Follicles at the temples, crown and front of the scalp tend to shrink. This is the same process behind male-pattern baldness [2]. It is slower to show than acne. It usually takes over twelve months to notice, and it can go on for as long as testosterone does [2].

Minoxidil, used on the scalp, is an option that is not a hormone. Australian product information says it is not known exactly how it works [7]. It seems to make the hair growth phase last longer [7]. Finasteride works in a different way. It blocks the enzyme that makes DHT in the scalp [6]. A small review of trans men taking low-dose finasteride found some improvement [2]. They did not have the sexual side effects reported in cisgender men on the same drug. But the evidence is still limited [2]. Finasteride must not be used during pregnancy. This matters if a partner could become pregnant [2]. It also acts on the same pathway that drives the changes from testosterone. So some prescribers treat it as a trade-off to talk through, not a routine add-on [2]. Hair loss can also take over a year to appear. So it is reasonable to wait before you decide on treatment [2].
list: Finasteride and dutasteride are not general blockers. They are often added for scalp hair loss. Australian guidance says it is unclear if they add benefit [2]

body: Testosterone at gender-affirming doses does not reliably stop ovulation (the release of an egg). So periods can continue, especially in the first months of treatment [5]. On full-dose testosterone, periods usually stop within about six months [2]. This varies, and not everyone gets there on testosterone alone [2]. Testosterone is not contraception, even if your periods have stopped [2].

If periods continue and cause distress, there are three options [3]. One is to check whether the testosterone dose has reached its target. Another is a progestogen taken by mouth, such as norethisterone or medroxyprogesterone acetate. The third is a levonorgestrel intrauterine device (IUD) [3]. Norethisterone is taken as tablets [8]. Medroxyprogesterone acetate comes as tablets, or as an injection given every three months [9]. The IUD is put in once and can stay in place for several years [10]. The IUD and the three-monthly medroxyprogesterone injection also work as contraception. Norethisterone and medroxyprogesterone tablets do not [2][8][9].

Testosterone lowers the oestrogen your ovaries make. The lining of the vagina needs oestrogen to stay thick and moist. With less oestrogen, the tissue can get thinner and drier, as in menopause. This can cause irritation, dryness or pain with penetration [5]. It tends to build up slowly over time on testosterone, rather than appear suddenly.

Low-dose vaginal oestrogen treats the tissue directly. It is used daily for the first two weeks, then twice a week [11]. Product information says very little gets into the blood, so blood oestradiol stays within the usual range after menopause [11]. It acts only where it is used. It does not work against the effects of testosterone in the rest of the body [5]. Vaginal moisturisers do not need a prescription. Some people try them first, as an option that is not a hormone [2].

These three sections are for people taking oestrogen, an androgen blocker, or both. Micronised progesterone is part of estradiol-based hormone therapy, not an add-on. It is covered in the [doses guide](#/doses#sec-doses-3).

Oestrogen and androgen blockers lower the effect of testosterone on hair roots (follicles). So facial and body hair usually grows more slowly. The change is gradual, and is largest after one to two years [16]. Hormones work on body hair more than on facial hair. They cannot remove hair that has already grown, so many people also use hair removal [17][16].

Two androgen blockers used in Australia are also approved for unwanted hair growth (hirsutism) in women. They are spironolactone [12] and cyproterone acetate [13]. If you already take one as part of estradiol-based therapy, it is already working on hair growth. It is not usually added a second time for hair.

Shaving, waxing and hair-removal creams are temporary. Laser hair removal and electrolysis give longer-lasting results, but need several sessions [17]. They are procedures, not medicines, so they are not on the PBS [17][18]. Medicare has no item for hair removal [17][18]. You pay for them yourself, and Australian guidance says they are costly [17][18]. If you take isotretinoin for acne, the product information says to avoid waxing, dermabrasion and laser treatment [14]. This applies during the course and for five to six months after it [14].
list: Body hair usually slows more than facial hair. The largest change is after one to two years [16][17]
Spironolactone and cyproterone are approved for unwanted hair growth in women. They are already part of many estradiol-based treatment plans [12][13]
Laser and electrolysis are procedures, not prescriptions. There is no Medicare or PBS cover, so you pay for them yourself [17][18]
On isotretinoin, wait five to six months after the course before laser or waxing [14]
sections.note: Hormones keep slowing hair growth for one to two years. Ask your prescriber when it makes sense to start or plan hair removal [16].

body: Male-pattern scalp hair loss is driven by DHT (dihydrotestosterone). The body makes DHT from testosterone, using an enzyme called 5-alpha reductase [6][2]. Oestrogen and an androgen blocker lower testosterone, which removes much of that drive. So further hair loss often slows or stops [17][16]. Australian guidance says spironolactone and cyproterone have been shown to improve it [17][16].

Minoxidil, used on the scalp, is an option that is not a hormone. Australian product information says it is not known exactly how it works [7]. It seems to make the hair growth phase last longer [7]. If it spreads from the scalp, it can cause unwanted hair on other parts of the body, such as the face. So wash your hands well after you put it on [7].

Finasteride and dutasteride block 5-alpha reductase. They are not general androgen blockers. They are often added for scalp hair loss. But Australian guidance says it is unclear if they add benefit [17]. Finasteride lowers the results of a prostate blood test called PSA (prostate-specific antigen) [6]. In studies of older men it lowered PSA by about half, and by less in younger men [6]. If you have prostate testing, tell the person who orders it [6]. This applies to anyone with a prostate. The product information also lists depression among effects reported after the medicine went on sale [6]. It also lists loss of libido (sex drive) that can continue after stopping [6].
list: Estradiol-based therapy itself often slows or stops scalp hair loss [17][16]
Minoxidil is not a hormone. Wash your hands after use to avoid unwanted facial hair [7]
Finasteride or dutasteride: it is unclear if they add benefit on top of estradiol-based therapy [17]
Finasteride lowers PSA results, by about half in studies of older men and less in younger men. Tell whoever orders a prostate test [6]
sections.note: Each of these medicines has its own page in the Medicines A–Z with doses, side effects and cost.

body: Oestrogen and androgen blockers can lower libido, or sex drive. They can also mean fewer erections that happen on their own. Erections can be harder to get or keep. Some people welcome these changes. For others, they cause distress [15].

Australia's 2026 standards of care describe several options. These include a lower dose of oestrogen or of the blocker. They also include sildenafil or tadalafil, which help erections but not sex drive. Low-dose testosterone may be used in some situations. You and your prescriber weigh each one against your own goals [15]. The full list is on the [Fertility, PrEP and surgery](#/related-care#sec-related-care-1) page, in the section on sexual function.
list: A lower dose of the blocker or oestrogen. This may bring back some effects of testosterone [15]
Sildenafil or tadalafil: these help erections, not sex drive [15]
Low-dose testosterone after orchidectomy or with full suppression, guided by blood tests. Low-dose testosterone cream on the genitals for penile pain, based on clinical experience [15]
